primary: In captive psittacine birds, does environmental or foraging enrichment reduce feather-damaging behaviour and stereotypic behaviour compared with unenriched housing or the pre-enrichment baseline?
secondary: Does enrichment increase foraging and exploratory behaviour?

Do effects differ by enrichment type (foraging devices, physical complexity, social or sensory enrichment) and between preventive use in young birds and therapeutic use in birds with established feather damage?
Does enrichment change glucocorticoid concentrations (plasma, faecal or feather corticosterone)?
hypotheses: H1: Enrichment reduces feather-damaging behaviour and stereotypies (pooled SMD below zero).
H2: Foraging enrichment has a larger effect than non-foraging enrichment.

pico.definition: Captive psittacine birds (Psittaciformes) of any species, age and sex, kept as companions, in research colonies, zoos, breeding facilities, rescue or rehabilitation centres.

Environmental enrichment: foraging enrichment (foraging devices, food puzzles, food that must be extracted, scattered or hidden), physical complexity (perches, manipulable and destructible objects), social, sensory or cognitive enrichment.
Unenriched or standard housing (food bowl, barren cage), or the pre-enrichment baseline in within-subject designs.

Primary: feather-damaging behaviour (plumage condition score or frequency/duration of feather picking) and stereotypic behaviour (frequency, duration or proportion of time). Secondary: foraging and exploratory behaviour, other abnormal behaviours, glucocorticoids, adverse events.
Controlled studies with a concurrent control group, or within-subject designs with a baseline or alternating conditions, with at least 3 birds.

inclusion: Enriched condition compared with an unenriched condition or baseline.
At least one eligible outcome reported quantitatively for each condition.
exclusion: Wild free-living psittacines, and non-psittacine birds (poultry, passerines, raptors).
Pharmacological or medical treatments of feather damage without an enrichment arm.
Studies of enrichment preference or use only, without an outcome measured under enriched and unenriched conditions.
Single-bird case reports; reviews, editorials and book chapters without original data; conference abstracts without data; duplicate reports.

abstract_completion.when: before release, or after release only for records without any decision

stages.maybe_rule: maybe only when no checklist item is clearly failed and a decisive item cannot be judged from title/abstract; maybe from either reviewer proceeds to full text
stages.no_abstract_rule: judge on title and keywords; exclude only if an item is clearly failed, otherwise maybe

calibration.new_round: next records of the fixed random order, same size

low_prevalence_rule.condition: prevalence paradox (low prevalence of non-excluded records, <10% or <5 non-excluded)

anti_stall_exits.exit_1_guarantor_adjudication: 20-30 min guided error autopsy and formal homologation by guarantor when agreement >= 88% and PABAK >= 0.60
anti_stall_exits.exit_2_enriched_round: 20-30 balanced records with ~30-40% known eligible/validation studies
anti_stall_exits.safety_net: any record marked maybe or include by either reviewer advances to full text

calibration.fallback: dual screening of all records without stopping rule, all disagreements resolved; reported as deviation
calibration.feedback: written, clear errors only, without disclosing who decided what

prioritisation.tool: active learning built into the group's screening platform (TF-IDF + multinomial naive Bayes, equal class priors, one model per reviewer, retrained every 10 decisions)
prioritisation.prior_knowledge: each reviewer's labels for the calibration sample (+1 validation-set study if no relevant record)

quality_check.sample: 10% of records reached by neither reviewer, minimum 100 (or all)
quality_check.on_hit: resume screening until 100 consecutive irrelevant, then repeat check

prioritisation.reference: SAFE procedure (Boetje and van de Schoot 2024)

risk_of_bias.rule: SYRCLE's risk of bias tool (Hooijmans et al. 2014) is applied to all included studies. For within-subject designs (baseline-intervention-baseline, ABA or crossover), the items on sequence generation and allocation concealment are judged on the order of conditions (randomised or counterbalanced versus fixed), and carry-over and habituation are recorded under 'other sources of bias'.

synthesis.model: A random-effects model is used for all analyses, with the between-study variance estimated by restricted maximum likelihood (REML) and 95% confidence intervals computed with the Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman method (IntHout et al. 2014), using the ad hoc correction that prevents intervals narrower than the standard Wald-type interval. When a study contributes several comparisons or doses that share a control group, a multilevel model with comparisons nested within studies is used (metafor::rma.mv). Heterogeneity is quantified with tau-squared and I-squared (Higgins and Thompson 2002) and summarised with 95% prediction intervals (Riley et al. 2011); Cochran's Q is reported descriptively and not used to choose the model.
comparisons: C1: any enrichment versus no enrichment (overall and by enrichment type).
C2: foraging versus non-foraging enrichment (indirect comparison by subgroup).
effect_measures: Feather damage and stereotypies: SMD (Hedges g), negative values favour enrichment.
Foraging and exploration: SMD, positive values favour enrichment.
subgroups: preventive (healthy birds) versus therapeutic (established feather damage)
body size group (small versus large psittacines)
sensitivity: exclusion of studies at high risk of bias (or with an overall judgement other than low)
exclusion of data converted, estimated or digitised from figures (e.g., means from medians, values read from plots)
exclusion of preprints, theses and other non-peer-reviewed reports
DerSimonian-Laird estimator with Wald-type confidence intervals instead of REML with Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman
assumed pre-post correlation of 0.3 and 0.7 for within-subject designs
exclusion of studies without blinded or video-based outcome assessment
special: Within-subject designs (baseline-intervention, ABA, crossover) are eligible because they dominate this literature. Their effect sizes are computed as standardised mean differences for paired data (change-score standardisation using the pre-intervention standard deviation, with an assumed pre-post correlation of 0.5 when it is not reported and 0.3 and 0.7 in sensitivity analyses), and designs are analysed together and separately (subgroup: between-subject versus within-subject).

When the animal is not the experimental unit (group-housed animals sharing an enrichment, or tanks), the effect size and its variance are based on the number of independent units, or the sample size is reduced by the design effect when only animal-level data are reported.
When several abnormal behaviours are reported, feather damage and stereotypies are analysed separately; the other behaviours are summarised narratively.
synthesis.publication_bias: When at least 10 studies contribute to an analysis, small-study effects are examined with contour-enhanced funnel plots and Egger's regression test for continuous outcomes (Egger et al. 1997) or Peters' test for binary outcomes (Peters et al. 2006); trim-and-fill is used only as a sensitivity analysis (Duval and Tweedie 2000). Selective outcome reporting is assessed within the risk-of-bias tools and by comparing reported outcomes with methods sections and available protocols or theses.
synthesis.certainty: The certainty of evidence for each primary and key secondary outcome is rated with GRADE (Guyatt et al. 2008) as high, moderate, low or very low. Evidence from randomised animal experiments starts at high certainty and from non-randomised studies at low certainty, and is rated down for risk of bias, inconsistency (judged mainly on prediction intervals), indirectness (e.g., laboratory versus field conditions, surrogate outcomes), imprecision and publication bias; non-randomised evidence may be rated up for large effects or dose-response gradients. Summary-of-findings tables are prepared with GRADEpro GDT.
synthesis.r_core:
es <- escalc(measure = "SMD", m1i = mean_t, sd1i = sd_t, n1i = n_t,
             m2i = mean_c, sd2i = sd_c, n2i = n_c, data = subset(d, outcome_id == "O1" & design == "between"))
esw <- escalc(measure = "SMCR", m1i = mean_t, m2i = mean_c, sd1i = sd_c, ni = n_t, ri = r_prepost, data = subset(d, outcome_id == "O1" & design == "within"))
all <- rbind(es, esw)
m <- rma.mv(yi, vi, random = ~ 1 | study/comparison, data = all, method = "REML", test = "t")
meta1 <- metagen(TE = yi, seTE = sqrt(vi), studlab = study, data = all, sm = "SMD",
                 method.tau = "REML", method.random.ci = "HK", common = FALSE, prediction = TRUE, subgroup = design)
